options: Strong Pound, Imports Cheaper, Exports Dearer
Strong Pound, Imports Costly, Exports Discounted
Stable Prices Increase Company Export Demand
Strong Prices Imply Cheaper Export Delivery
questions.why: It works for any currency: a stronger home currency makes imports cheaper and exports dearer abroad.
whyNot: The effects run the other way round in that version.
That is not the mnemonic.
That is not the mnemonic.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines hedging?
options: Using arrangements such as a forward contract to fix a future exchange rate
Buying a foreign currency in the hope that it will rise
Pricing all sales in the customer's currency
Holding cash reserves in case of a downturn
questions.why: Hedging removes the uncertainty and also removes any benefit from a favourable movement.
whyNot: That is speculation.
That increases exposure rather than reducing it.
That is a liquidity precaution.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a skill shortage?
options: A situation in which employers cannot find enough workers with the skills they need
A situation in which there are more workers than jobs
A shortage of training providers in a country
A situation in which wages are falling
questions.why: Skill shortages raise wage costs, constrain output and can delay or prevent expansion.
whyNot: That is unemployment.
Limited provision is one cause, not the definition.
Shortages tend to raise wages.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a forward contract?
options: An agreement to exchange currency at a fixed rate on a set future date
A contract to deliver goods before payment is received
An agreement to buy goods at next year's market price
A loan denominated in a foreign currency
questions.why: It fixes the rate, which removes the uncertainty at a cost.
whyNot: That is a trade credit arrangement.
That is a variable-price supply contract.
That is foreign currency borrowing.

questions.stem: A product sells for $60 and the rate moves from EUR1 = $1.10 to EUR1 = $1.25. What is the revenue per unit in euros after the change?
whyNot: That is the revenue before the change.
That multiplies rather than divides.
That uses an incorrect calculation.

questions.stem: Revenue per unit falls from EUR54.55 to EUR48.00 on 40,000 units. What is the annual effect?
options: A fall of about EUR262,000
A fall of about EUR6.55
A fall of about EUR1,920,000
No effect, because the dollar price is unchanged
whyNot: That is the effect per unit, not the annual total.
That is total revenue after the change, not the fall.
The euro value of the same dollar price has fallen.

questions.stem: To protect euro revenue of EUR54.55 at a rate of EUR1 = $1.25, what dollar price is needed?
questions.why: 54.55 x 1.25 = $68.19, a price increase of 13.6% to the customer.
whyNot: That is the original price, which no longer yields EUR54.55.
That divides instead of multiplying.
That is the euro figure, not a dollar price.

questions.stem: A home currency depreciates. What happens to an importer of inputs?
options: Input costs rise and margins are squeezed
Input costs fall and margins improve
There is no effect on input costs
Input costs fall only if the inputs are perishable
questions.why: SPICED works in reverse: a weaker currency makes imports dearer.
whyNot: That is the effect of an appreciation.
Imported inputs are directly affected.
Perishability is irrelevant to currency effects.

questions.stem: Which management response removes currency exposure rather than insuring against it?
options: Producing in the market where you sell, so costs and revenues are in the same currency
Buying a forward contract
Adding a margin to the price for currency movement
Accepting the risk and monitoring it
questions.why: This is the natural hedge, and it is the most robust answer because the exposure is eliminated.
whyNot: A forward contract insures against the movement for one transaction.
A margin absorbs the risk rather than removing it.
Accepting the risk leaves the exposure in place.

questions.stem: Why is a business that both imports inputs and exports output partly hedged already?
options: A depreciation raises its input costs and its export revenue at the same time
Importing and exporting are taxed at the same rate
Currency movements do not affect physical goods
Its bank automatically offsets the two flows
questions.why: Working out the net exposure is what a good answer does rather than treating the business as purely one or the other.
whyNot: Tax treatment is unrelated.
Traded goods are precisely what is affected.
No bank does this automatically.

questions.stem: Whether an exporter can pass on a currency-driven price rise depends most on what?
options: Price elasticity of demand and whether competitors share the same currency
The size of the business's marketing budget
The exchange rate regime in the destination country
The volume of its domestic sales
questions.why: If competitors are also based in the appreciating currency, all of them face the same pressure and the price can be raised.
whyNot: Marketing spend does not determine whether a price rise sticks.
The regime matters less than the level and competitors' positions.
Domestic volume does not affect the export decision directly.

questions.stem: Why can exchange rate volatility hurt more than a permanently unfavourable level?
options: A contract priced today and settled later can lose its whole margin to a movement nobody controls
Volatility raises the average exchange rate over time
Volatility is always accompanied by inflation
A permanently unfavourable level has no effect on competitiveness
questions.why: A permanently strong currency is a disadvantage a business can adapt to; volatility prevents planning at all.
whyNot: Volatility concerns variation, not the average.
The two are not necessarily linked.
A permanently unfavourable level does affect competitiveness.

questions.stem: What is the most serious effect of a skill shortage on a business?
options: Expansion is delayed or abandoned even though the market opportunity exists
The business must pay its existing staff less
The business is prevented from advertising vacancies
The business must relocate its head office
questions.why: A resort's expansion plans can be constrained by the inability to staff a new property rather than by finance or demand.
whyNot: Shortages bid wages up, not down.
Advertising vacancies is unrestricted.
Relocation is one possible response, not an automatic effect.

questions.stem: Which response to a skill shortage removes the need for the skill altogether?
options: Automation
Training internally
Recruiting internationally
Raising pay to improve retention
questions.why: Each option has a cost: training is slow and the trained staff may leave, international recruitment depends on immigration rules, and higher pay treats the symptom.
whyNot: Training supplies the skill rather than removing the need.
That imports the skill.
That retains people who already have it.

questions.stem: Why is a resort in an import-dependent island economy unusually well hedged on the cost side?
options: Revenue is largely earned in foreign currency and most inputs are paid for in foreign currency too
It has no costs denominated in any currency
Tourism revenue is fixed by government
Imported goods are exempt from currency movements
questions.why: The remaining exposure sits mainly in the local-currency costs, chiefly wages.
whyNot: All businesses have costs in some currency.
Prices are set commercially.
Imports are directly affected by currency movements.

questions.stem: How should the decision to hedge or relocate depend on the nature of the currency movement?
options: Hedge a temporary movement; consider local production for a permanent one
Always hedge, whatever the cause of the movement
Always relocate, because hedging costs money
Neither, because currency movements cannot be managed
questions.why: Hedging suits short-term uncertainty; a structural change in competitiveness calls for a structural response.
whyNot: Hedging a permanent shift merely delays the problem.
Relocation is a very large commitment for a temporary movement.
Several management options exist.
